messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At twenty-one, Elias had spent fourteen months as a relief worker navigating a fractured conflict zone. The memory of his final convoy remains sharply etched in his mind: a sudden ambush that split their vehicles, the sharp crack of rifle fire echoing off canyon walls, and the chaotic shouts of soldiers speaking rapidly in Arabic as they dragged wounded bodies into the dust. He had stood frozen, watching boots stomp and weapons shift, utterly powerless to stop what was unfolding. The sheer, visceral chaos of that afternoon left a deep psychological imprint, which explains why certain ordinary cues now pierce through his defenses like shrapnel. When Elias returned to his parish as a social ministry worker, the past began to reinvade his daily life. If a colleague mentioned troop movements, listened to a colleague recount the event, or caught a sudden shout in Arabic from a passing street vendor, those triggers immediately dragged the old scene back into his awareness. He could feel the memory tightening around his ribs, the story so extreme it was difficult to accept it had actually happened to him. Yet remembering it brought back the same terror he felt at the time, making it feel like it was happening right now rather than something that was over. That rushing sense of the past colliding with the present instantly put his body on high alert; the memory did not stay contained but immediately sharpened his threat system, making him scan the room for danger. Even routine interactions in the ministry office now carried weight. A sudden movement by a visitor or a raised voice at the news desk put him immediately on guard, his pulse spiking before he could register any actual risk. This heightened state of readiness then fed directly back into his recall; the mere anticipation of danger kept his mind fixed on the original ambush, making the memory feel inescapable and continuously present. To cope with the relentless intrusion of those memories and the constant low hum of danger, Elias had developed quiet but rigid habits over several months. The auditory trigger of shouting in Arabic, whether from a tense radio broadcast or a crowded street, immediately pushed him toward his maladaptive strategies. He began telling himself he had to stay up until very late, as if forcing himself to remain conscious might somehow intercept a recurrence. When the rumination set in, his mind cycled relentlessly through the tactical decisions of that afternoon, obsessing over how the event could have been prevented if only different boots had walked that path. This exhaustion and mental fatigue remained contained within his coping habits; he started avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful, convincing himself that joy was a luxury he did not deserve while others still suffered. The weight of these coping habits kept the traumatic memory perpetually active, as the late nights and endless mental rehearsals ensured the past never had the chance to fade into history. His physical vigilance had become a self-sustaining current. Waking during the night to check whether he was safe, Elias would lie rigid in his marital bed, listening to every creak of the house, convinced the outside world was closing in. This perpetual state of checking left him emotionally drained, making him hyper-sensitive to ordinary triggers whenever he stepped outside the church. When a stranger approached him to ask for directions, the mere proximity felt like an incursion, his body bracing against an imaginary threat that had no name. That defensive posture only deepened the memory’s hold; the constant scanning made the original ambush feel like it was happening again, refusing to be processed as something that had already ended. He had come to believe that the only way to survive was to remain perpetually braced, even as his avoidance of hopeful moments and chronic exhaustion quietly eroded his connection to his wife, leaving him isolated in the very community he worked to serve. What finally brought Elias to seek professional help was the morning he found himself unable to leave his home after hearing a sudden shout in Arabic from a passing street vendor. He had grown terrified of the loop tightening around his days, where every flash of fear pulled him back into the dust of the convoy, and every attempt to rest only made the terror return sharper. He was most afraid of losing the fragile stability he had fought to build, yet he deeply hoped to find a way to finally let the past rest and reclaim the life he had left behind.
